Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I call to order the second meeting of the Global Conference on Promoting Interreligious and Intercultural Dialogue and Tolerance in Countering Hate Speech. I hope that you've had an excellent lunch break and that we will be able to resume ahead with the list of speakers. I have the pleasure now of giving the floor to Ambassador Yojna Patel, Deputy Permanent Representative of India. You have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. We meet at a difficult moment in history. Discriminatory rhetoric based on gender, race, ethnicity, or religious identity is corroding the bonds that hold societies together, and in some instances, stoking violent conflict. My delegation is acutely aware of this issue. Indians across the world increasingly face hateful rhetoric online and offline for the color of our skin, our faith, our dress, our food, and our status as migrant workers. The problem is compounded by technology. The flood of information makes it hard for citizens to distinguish real from fabricated content, a gap bad actors exploit to sow chaos. Social media's engagement-driven algorithms amplify negative content while anonymity and the absence of meaningful consequences emboldens individuals. In its most extreme form, online hostility escalates into incitement, violence, and civil unrest, even as it is skillfully used to radicalize impressionable youth towards extremism and terrorism. Combating hate speech is thus vital in today's hyper-connected world. Chair, while inter-religious dialogue and tolerance matter, hate speech goes beyond religion and calls for a change in attitude and understanding. We believe this requires a multi-pronged approach. This must begin first with education. Teaching children to value their own heritage while respecting others, to engage respectfully in dialogue lays the early foundations for mutual understanding. Secondly, clear and stringent laws that protect free speech while punishing incitement are essential. India's criminal laws precisely target those who stir hostility between communities or harm religious sensibilities and forbid circulating material designed to inflame communal tensions. Third, the greatest bulwark against intolerance is the checks and balances of democracy. A pluralistic society where every religion is guaranteed freedom and respect is essential for social harmony. Fourth, preventing the weaponization of digital technology is critical to combating hate speech. India's IT laws obligate social media companies to maintain robust content policies appoint grievance officers, respond to complaints within a day, resolve them within strict timelines, and trace the originators of inflammatory content. Chair, India's centuries-long experience of diverse faiths, languages, and cultures living side by side embodies a culture of tolerance and respect. We remain committed to promoting intercultural and inter-religious cooperation across all sections of society to effectively combat hate speech. Thank you.

I thank Ambassador and Deputy Permanent Representative of the Russian Federation, and I now give the floor to His Excellency Michael Christian Gort, Ambassador and Deputy Permanent Representative of Canada.

President, Canada is honoured to participate in this global conference dedicated to promoting interreligious and intercultural dialogue, as well as tolerance. As a diverse and pluralistic society, Canada believes diversity to be one of its greatest strengths. However, diversity alone does not guarantee inclusion. Social cohesion must be fueled by mutual respect, comprehension, and dialogue between peoples of different confessions, cultures, and origins. We meet at a time when polarization, intolerance, discrimination, and hatred are on the rise in numerous societies, largely due to disinformation and misinformation spread by algorithms on various technology platforms. Current conflicts have also increased hostilities towards religious and minority communities.

When people are made to feel that they do not belong because of their faith, culture, or identity, the harm extends beyond individuals. It weakens the social cohesion that binds our communities together. Canada has experienced these challenges firsthand. Attacks targeting places of worship and schools, along with rising incidents motivated by hate and intolerance, remind us that vigilance and action remain essential. Canada is committed to building a safer and more inclusive society by combating all forms of racism, discrimination, and intolerance, including Islamophobia, anti-Semitism, and other forms of hate. This work is supported by initiatives such as Canada's Anti-Racism Strategy and Action Plan on Combating Hate. We have also established a new advisory council on rights, equality, and inclusion, bringing together experts and community leaders to strengthen social cohesion, promote inclusion, and help counter racism and hate. Its work is grounded in a simple belief: far more unites us than divides us. International cooperation is equally important. Human Rights Council resolution 16/18 remains a valuable framework for promoting respect, protecting freedom of religion or belief, and addressing intolerance through practical action. Excellencies, colleagues, hate and racism have no place in our societies. Promoting tolerance means building inclusive and resilient societies where every person feels respected, valued, and able to contribute fully. Canada stands ready to work with member states, faith leaders, civil societies, and communities around the world to advance dialogue, strengthen social cohesion, and counter hate in all its forms. Together, we must choose coexistence over division, dignity over discrimination, and inclusion over hate. I thank you.
I thank the Ambassador and Permanent Representative of Canada, and I now give the floor to His Excellency Mohamed Fathid Ahmed Idris, Ambassador and Permanent Observer of the African Union.

Thank you very much, my dear brother, Ambassador Omar, and through you, our appreciation to the King of Mufaro and His Excellency Minister for Foreign Affairs, Nasser Khouri, for inaugurating this important meeting, and our appreciation to His Excellency, High Representative, Under-Secretary Miguel Martinos, and the Alliance of Civilizations, and the Under-Secretary, Shaluka Bayani, Special Advisor for Secretary General on the Prevention of Genocide, and to the Office of Genocide Prevention and Responsibility to Protect. I speak for the African Union Commission, and I want to emphasize that dialogue and tolerance run through our founding texts. The African Charter on Human and People's Rights guarantees freedom of consciousness and religion and pairs free expression with an individual duty of tolerance and respect for fellow beings without discrimination. The Charter of the African Cultural Renaissance makes dialogue among cultures continental policy. Agenda 2063 promises an Africa of shared values and a common heritage. Practice came before texts. Religious shrines share the same streets in most African sites and cities. And the idea that many of our societies call Ubuntu, that a person is a person through other person, is tolerance lived as daily habit. The Union African Union works to keep it so. Our citizens and diaspora directorate convenes African dialogue religious leaders in a continental interfaith dialogue platform. And our mediators draw routinely on religious and traditional authority in reconciliation work. Where dialogue fails, we see the cost easily and early. The Peace and Security Council holds an open session each year on preventing the ideology of genocide and the hate crimes. And our early warning system reads hate speeches as a risk factor and indicator of atrocity crimes. In Luanda, three weeks ago, Our Assembly adopted a decision and action plan placing prevention at the center of the Union's peace and security work. Countering hate speech is prevention practiced early. Terrorism has no religion, and African faith communities, among its principal victims, remain among the most credible voices against it. The chairperson of the African Commission has condemned in plain terms xenophobic violence against African migrants. The hatred follows our people abroad. The Union treats its diaspora as a sixth region, and the second International Decade for People of African Descent belongs on this conference's agenda. Two requests. Take the Secretary-General's strategy and the plan of action on hate speech to country level in partnership with the African Union and our regional economic communities, and count Africa's interfaith networks among its instruments. And second, close the digital gap. Content moderation in African languages remains thin. while algorithmic amplification rewards outrage. And the outcome of today should say so. In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, tolerance in the African Union's practice is an instrument of peace, and dialogue is how we keep it in working together. Thank you very much.

I thank the Ambassador and Permanent Observer of the African Union, His Excellency Mohamed Fathi Ahmed Idris, for his statement. And I now have the pleasure of giving the floor to Ms. Miriam Fariva Naim, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of the Maldives.

Thank you, Ambassador. Apathy and hate are the counterthesis of unity and cooperation. and hate speech is spreading at an alarming speed and scale. Technologies that have enabled instantaneous connections between cultures have also amplified hateful narratives that target people based on faith, race, or culture. These ideas cross borders in seconds, deepening divisions within and between societies, and creating excuses for violence and atrocity crimes. Every person should be free to shape their own future. Hate speech shrinks that freedom by turning identity into a reason for exclusion. Interreligious and intercultural dialogue is an instrument of prevention. It helps communities to challenge falsehoods, resolve differences peacefully, and build the kind of trust supported by international human rights law on which resilient societies depend. Education must also remain central. Our schools should foster respect, empathy, critical thinking, and digital literacy from an early age. Young people must be equipped to recognize misinformation and to respond to hatred with knowledge. Technology companies and social media platforms carry greater responsibility. They must prevent their services from being exploited to spread incitement and hatred. The Maldives welcomes the International Day to Combat Islamophobia and the appointment of the United Nations Special Envoy. We also welcome work towards a United Nations plan of action. These initiatives must lead to measurable action. Attempts to associate Islam or any religion with terrorism and violent extremism are false and dangerous. Such narratives fuel discrimination, attacks against individuals and places of worship, and, as in the case of the Palestinian people, the dehumanization of an entire population, culminating in the current genocide. Governments, community leaders, educators, and civil society must work together in our response to counter hate speech. The Maldives reaffirms its commitment to confronting all forms of religious hatred and discrimination. Let us replace suspicion with understanding, division with dialogue, and hatred with respect for our common humanity. In doing so, we defend the freedom of every person and community to shape their own future. I thank you.

I thank the representative of the Maldives. I have the pleasure now of giving the floor to His Excellency Mr. Sun Li, Ambassador and Deputy Permanent Representative of China. You have the floor, Ambassador.

Your Excellencies, Ambassador Hilali, Special Bihani, High Representative Moratino. While safeguarding the freedom of expression, we must counter disinformation and hate speech, both online and offline, in accordance with the law. Colleagues, for over 5,000 years, the Chinese nation has consistently pursued and carried forward the ideals of peace, amity and harmony. China has translated the civilizational wisdom of harmony and coexistence into a global governance approach, upholding a vision of civilization based on equality, mutual learning and dialogue, and inclusiveness, actively implementing the global civilization initiative put forward by President Xi Jinping, establishing and commemorating the International Day for Dialogue Among Civilizations at the UN, and promoting exchanges and dialogue among the world's different civilizations to advance world peace and development. I thank Ambassador and Deputy Permanent Representative of China for that statement. I now give the floor to Ms. Hedda Samson, Ambassador, Deputy Head of the Delegation of the European Union.

Thank you, Mr. President, distinguished delegates, colleagues. I have the honor to speak on behalf of the European Union and its Member States. The candidate countries North Macedonia, Montenegro, Albania, the Republic of Moldova, as well as Armenia, Andorra, San Marino, and the United Kingdom, aligned themselves with this statement. Thanks to the UN Alliance of Civilizations, the UN Office on Genocide Prevention and the Responsibility to Protect, and the Kingdom of Morocco for bringing us together today. We are joined in a belief that inter-religious and inter-cultural dialogue are essential tools in breaking down barriers and building understanding. Diversity is a core value of the European Union. And the EU actively supports initiatives which foster tolerance, cultural diversity and religious pluralism. And we do this because it's the right thing to do. but also because we know how poisonous hate speech can be in our societies, both offline and, increasingly, online. Hate speech is a cross-cutting phenomenon, and as such it needs to be tackled with a comprehensive approach. That means tackling all grounds of discrimination and violence, including religious or belief, sexual orientation or gender identity, ethnicity, nationality, caste, or disability, extending to persons belonging to national or ethnic, religious, and linguistic minorities. It also involves engaging with diverse faiths, beliefs, and philosophical or cultural communities. And the EU does this through its structured dialogues with churches, religious associations, and non-confessional organizations. We work with them, as with member states, international organizations, EU agencies, and civil society. Because only together are we best able to ensure respect for human rights, freedom, democracy, equality, rule of law, and dignity. This involves recognising the right of everyone to have, or not to have, a religion or belief, to change it or to manifest it, alone or in community with others, in public or private. The EU condemns any form of discrimination, intolerance, violence and persecution based on grounds of religion or belief, and rejects any form of incitement to religious hatred. At the same time, we stand for both the right to freedom of religion or belief and the freedom of opinion and expression, which extends to information and ideas that may offend, shock or disturb others, including criticism of religion, ideology, beliefs and institutions. Any restriction on freedom of religion or belief or freedom of expression must be provided by law, may only be imposed for the grounds set out in international human rights law, and must conform to the strict tests of necessity and proportionality. Putting these things together, the EU has built action to combat hate speech into all of our strategies on combating discrimination, from that on racism to that on gender. Specifically, the EU is also committed to tailored, practical action to combat hate speech based on religion or belief, through the work of the Europe-wide coordinators on combating anti-Muslim hatred and anti-Semitism. Ten years ago, in 2016, the EU established a High-Level Group on Combating Hate Speech and Hate Crime. This has actively promoted cooperation between public authorities and civil society organisations through the drawing up of key guiding principles on cooperation between law enforcement authorities and civil society organizations. And underpinning this work, the European Commission provides financial support to national authorities and civil society organizations working on hate speech through its program on citizens, equality, rights, and values. These are practical expressions of our effective commitment to promoting interreligious and intercultural dialogue and tolerance in countering hate speech. And we shall continue to work with partners to this effect. I thank you.
I thank the Ambassador and Deputy Head of Delegation of the European Union. I now give the floor to To Ukraine, Mr. Andriy Baziw, Councillor at the Mission of Ukraine. You have the floor, sir.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Hate speech does not exist in a vacuum. It prepares the ground for discrimination and violence. And when hatred is given religious sanction, its destructive power becomes even greater. For Ukraine, these are not abstract concerns. For years, Russia has systematically weaponized religion to justify its war of aggression against our country. The ideology of the so-called Russian world portrays Russia as the defender of the supposedly besieged civilization and depicts Ukraine and the rest of democratic world as morally alien and hostile. The hierarchy of the Russian Orthodox Church has provided this ideology with religious language and legitimacy. Russia's Orthodox chief Kirill has repeatedly justified Russia's aggression and portrayed participation in the war as a spiritual duty. In 2024, the World Russian People's Council, under his chairmanship, went so far as to describe Russia's war against Ukraine as a holy war. These are not words of peacemakers. They turn religion into an instrument of mobilizing society for aggression. dehumanizing its victims and presenting violence as morally righteous. The World Council of Churches has condemned Russia's misuse of religious language and authority to justify armed aggression and hatred. The consequences are measured not only in words, though. During its war against Ukraine, Russia has destroyed or damaged more than 800 religious sites in our country. More than 80 clergy and religious servants have been killed. Churches, prayer houses, synagogues, mosques, and other religious sites belonging to different denominations have suffered from Russian attacks. Just three months ago, another massive Russian attack severely damaged the Dormition Cathedral of the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, one of the most important Orthodox sanctuaries in Eastern Europe and a UNESCO World Heritage site. In the territories temporarily occupied by Russia, the same ideology is translated into repression. Independent religious communities face intimidation, arbitrary detention, torture, forced incorporation into Russian-controlled religious structures. Russia has forcibly absorbed into the Russian Orthodox Church eight dioceses of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church. Other communities, including Protestants, Muslims, Jehovah's Witnesses, have been subjected to Russia's repressive legislation and persecution. Against this background, Russia's allegations of religion persecution in Ukraine are particularly cynical. Ukraine does not ban a faith or interfere with anyone's right to worship. Our legislation addresses institutional affiliation with the Russian Orthodox Church. an organization whose leadership openly supports and provides religious justification for aggression. The law provides for an individualized legal procedure and opportunity to sever such affiliation and judicial review. Freedom of religion must be protected without exception, but it cannot be invoked to shield foreign interference or institutions serving as instruments of the aggressor state. I thank you, Mr. Chair.

Thank you.

Thank you very much, Excellency. The next segment of our conference is on voices of stakeholders. And these voices comprise UN entities, civil society, organizations, and faith actors. First of all, UN entities. May I invite her Excellency, Miss Melissa Fleming, Under-Secretary-General for Global Communications. She's not yet here, but when she does arrive, we'll give her the floor. So may I invite Mr. A. Noub Omoish, Director for Policy and Coordination, OCT.

when polarization, intolerance, and identity-based tensions affect so many societies. We cannot overstate the importance of dialogue and tolerance for more peaceful, inclusive, and resilient communities. From a counterterrorism perspective, interreligious and intercultural dialogue is not only a matter of social cohesion. It is also an important tool for preventing terrorism and tackling violent extremism conducive to terrorism. Terrorist actors and their narratives often exploit existing or perceived divisions, grievances, and exclusion. In some contexts, these narratives also draw on misogyny and other forms of gender-based discrimination, exploiting harmful gender stereotypes and grievances to mobilize support and reinforce exclusion. Hate speech can, in some circumstances, facilitate pathways to terrorism by deepening polarization, dehumanizing individuals and communities, and creating conditions in which violence appears easier to justify. Extremist groups often use narratives based on intolerance, discrimination, and hatred to incite, to recruit supporters, and rationalize acts of violence. The accelerated flow of information, increased global connectivity facilitated by digital platforms and artificial intelligence enable them to do so with unprecedented speed, scale, and reach. Not all manifestations of hate speech are linked to or conducive to terrorism. For that reason, it is critical that hate speech and terrorism-related conduct be clearly distinguished in law, policy, and practice at all stages of our responses, from design to implementation. And it is critical that efforts to address the conditions conducive to the spread of terrorism are fully compliant with international law. Because prevention is most effective when it strengthens social cohesion, promotes human rights and gender equality, and creates spaces where differences are considered constructively. Such approaches also reduce vulnerabilities that may otherwise be exploited for terrorist purposes. Thank you.
Thank you very much, Mr. Omoish. May I now invite Ms. Alexandra Fong, Deputy Director, Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs.

And I would also like to express our appreciation and our thanks to the organizers. Excellencies, from the perspective of the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, our work on our core mandates, political analysis, preventive diplomacy, peacemaking and peacebuilding is today incomplete if we do not take into account the broader information ecosystem and hate speech in particular. As many speakers have stressed throughout the day, the UN's efforts to tackle hate speech and disinformation are not new. We believe it was back in 1947 at the very third session that the General Assembly adopted a resolution condemning all forms of propaganda. And in that same year, the third committee was already discussing the prevention of the dissemination of slanderous statements, which are harmful to good relations between states. So of course, this has been underlined. The problem is not new. What has changed today and what we're grappling with is, of course, the scale, the speed and the ease of transmission of hate speech and disinformation to digital media. And now we have generative AI, which is transforming how information is created, how it is shared, how it is consumed, reshaping the landscape of hate speech at various stages, right from its creation through to its dissemination and amplification, detection and moderation. So how are we adapting and responding in our political work? Our primary focus is how hate speech affects the political processes, the peace processes, and the dialogue processes in which the UN is engaged. This, of course, takes many forms and so do possible responses. We have seen some interesting innovations and developments. Libya is an example in which the parties in the 2020 agreement included provisions to take action against hate speech and inflammatory rhetoric. We know that hate speech is often an early warning sign of deeper societal fractures, as has been stressed by speakers before me. Countering it requires not only technology, but trusted voices, political leadership, and dialogue. We are working to equip our envoys, our mediators, as well as their teams, with tools and expertise to support exactly this, to promote dialogue and to counter hate speech in their public advocacy as well as in their quiet engagements. We have a multidisciplinary approach to this and try and address these issues through a variety of avenues, notably mediation, peacebuilding, including through the Secretary-General's Peacebuilding Fund, which has been more and more active in this area, electoral assistance, and through our strategic communications. We're also working to better understand the gendered dimensions of hate speech. For instance, together with UN Women and other partners, we're really trying to help address a concerning trend of online harassment and discrimination faced by women electoral candidates. In some contexts, we have seen that this form of online harassment is pushing women out of public life. Given the complexity of all of this, working in partnership is, of course, essential, and this means strong partnerships within the UN, as well as with Member States, media, civil society, regional organizations, and specifically for our work, important groups such as the Network of Religious and Traditional Peacemakers, from whom we have learned a great deal in this area. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much, Director Ms. Alexandra Fong. We are still holding on for USG Melissa Fleming. When she arrives, she will take the floor. At this point in time, may I turn to civil society and faith actors. I have the privilege to invite Dr. Ahmed Shaheed, Professor of International Human Rights Law School of Law and Human Rights Centre, University of Essex.

Thank you, distinguished Chair, Your Excellencies, distinguished participants, partners and friends. I am honoured to join this high-level conference today. I thank the organisers for the kind invitation extended to me. I would like to highlight today three recent initiatives pursued by the Essex Human Rights Centre. These support the implementation of existing action plans and strategies in ways that uphold human rights and foster belonging and social cohesion. I refer to the Tirana Framework on countering all forms of intolerance, the Oslo Model for engaging with all levels of distributed governance for countering religious intolerance, and the Interdisciplinary Cronulla Declaration of Principles for countering Islamophobia and antisemitism. All these have been recognized in recent reports of the UN Secretary-General. The Tirana and Oslo initiatives seek to increase the scope and depth of the Istanbul process linked to the action plan and Human Rights Council resolution 1618. Building on good practice from previous Istanbul process meetings, Tirana offers a free-standing multi-stakeholder platform to increase transparency and shared learning among different actors while also supporting accountability. The Oslo Model draws on the good practices of UN treaty bodies that work with subnational authorities. It offers a multi-level structure for the whole society approach advocated by the UN Global Strategy and supports depolarization. It helps us to go beyond abstract normative debates and engage in real practical solutions. The Granada Declaration seeks to complement existing efforts to counter antisemitism and Islamophobia. It offers a framework to address gaps, omissions, and interactions in our current efforts, and supports inclusion and leadership by grounding our efforts in human rights. An increasing number of actors who work on all forms of hatred are stressing the value of shared approaches, such as the Pathways to Inclusion project, launched recently by the OSCE region with support from Canada. I invite all stakeholders to examine these initiatives and see how their efforts can benefit from using these three human rights-based tools. All three draw on various recommendations that I had offered to the UN in my reports between 2016 and 2022, as well as the UN Global Strategy, especially commitments numbers 4, 8, and 11. All three tools also rely on key insights from the 1995 UNESCO Declaration of Principles on Tolerance, especially its call for an inclusive and egalitarian approach and support for inclusion. I refer to the UNESCO principles today, given their relevance for building a society that fosters belonging, equal concern and respect, an active attitude of respect for diversity, and a practice that can build trust, solidarity, and norms of reciprocity. These are the core elements of social cohesion. The UNESCO declaration is therefore vital for the goals that have been set for today's conference. as per commitment number eight of the UN Global Strategy. May I therefore conclude by appealing to you all to breathe new life into the implementation of the UNESCO declaration as we mark 30th anniversary of its adoption by the UNGA in December this year and mobilize it to support the UN Global Strategy to combat all forms of hate. I thank you all.
Thank you very much, Professor Shahid. May I now invite Mr. El Mehdi Boudra, President Association Memonah, who will address us by video link.

Excellencies, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, it is an honor to take the floor at the Global Conference on Promoting Interreligious and Intercultural Dialogue and Tolerance in Countering Hate Speech. I would like to commend my country, the Kingdom of Morocco, for its leadership in promoting dialogue, convivencia, and mutual understanding as essential pillars of peace. At Association Mimouna, our experience has taught us a simple lesson. If hatred can be spread through narratives, then dialogue can also create powerful narratives of understanding and coexistence. For us, preserving Morocco's Jewish heritage means preserving who we are. In Morocco, this is not only the responsibility of those who inherited this heritage, it is the responsibility of every Moroccan. We are proud to be Muslim by faith, African, Amazigh, and Arab by identity, and deeply shaped by more than 2,000 years of Jewish presence and civilization in Morocco. Under the leadership of His Majesty King Mohammed VI, Morocco's diversity is recognized not as a threat to our identity, but as one of the greatest strengths. This vision is reflected in Morocco's 2000 constitution and has been translated into action through the restoration of Jewish heritage sites, the preservation of cemeteries, the rehabilitation of historic mellahs, and the creation of Bayt Dakhira in Essaouira. But heritage remains alive only when it is understood, shared, and transmitted. This is why education matters. In 2020, Morocco became the first country in the Arab world to include Jewish history and heritage in primary school curricula. The message is clear. The history of Moroccan Jews is not a separate chapter. It is part of the history of Morocco. This matters for young people whose understanding of different communities can increasingly be shaped by social media, polarization, and conflict. We must therefore turn awareness into action. Hate speech, antisemitism, Islamophobia, xenophobia, and other forms of identity-based hatred may target different communities, but they often grow from the same roots: stereotypes, misinformation, dehumanization, and the refusal to recognize the dignity of the other. We must invest in prevention through education, cultural heritage, youth exchange, interfaith dialogue, and people-to-people engagement. At Mimouna, we believe young people are not merely the audience, they are the answer. Founded by students nearly 20 years ago, Mimouna empowers young people to become storytellers of their own history and ambassador for dialogue and convivencia. But none of this can succeed alone. It requires partnership between government, religious leaders, educators, civil society, media, and above all, young people. In a world where hate speech can cross borders and reach millions within seconds, our response must also cross borders. Ultimately, our success should be measured by whether the next generation regardless of religion or ethnicity, sees the heritage of minorities community, not as the legacy of an absent past, but as an integral part of our shared history and identity.
